# 05: One error format, with the type URN as the sole discriminator

**What to build:** Every error this API can emit is an RFC 9457 problem document, and a
client branches on exactly one field: the `type` URN. Two fields that can disagree is
the failure mode this exists to prevent.

Use the framework's own problem-document support rather than a hand-rolled envelope. The
framework already emits problem documents for validation rejections, unsupported media
types, wrong methods and malformed JSON — a custom shape would be a *second* error
format, not a replacement.

Two additions on top of the default:

- **Field-level validation errors as an extension member.** The default packs every
  violation into one unusable sentence, which no form can mark up.
- **The `type` URNs as constants in `common`**, so the frontend's generated types and the
  backend agree on the vocabulary from one place.

`Retry-After` policy is part of this contract: present where retrying will help, absent
where it will not. Later tickets rely on that distinction being machine-readable.

**Blocked by:** 01

**Status:** ready-for-agent

- [ ] A validation failure returns a problem document with per-field detail, not one
      sentence
- [ ] Malformed JSON, an unsupported media type and a wrong method all return the same
      document shape
- [ ] Problem-type URNs live as constants in one place
- [ ] Tests cover the shape at the web layer without starting a database

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

A payment gateway that holds account balances and moves money between accounts, with currency conversion, idempotent retries, and downstream notification of other domain services.

## Language

### Accounts and money

**Account**:
An entity holding a balance in a single Currency, identified by an ID. It is the atomic entity of this context — nothing owns it.
_Avoid_: Wallet, User account

**User**:
A person who owns an Account. **Deliberately unmodelled** — named here so its absence reads as a decision rather than an oversight. Nothing in this context references a caller or an owner.
_Avoid_: Customer, Owner, Account holder

**Currency**:
One of the three denominations an Account's balance is held in: EUR, USD, HUF. Fixed at Account creation and immutable thereafter.

**Money**:
An amount paired with the Currency it is denominated in. There is no bare amount in this context; a number without a Currency is not Money.

**Minor Units**:
The indivisible sub-unit a Currency is counted in — cents for EUR and USD, fillér for HUF. All Money is counted in whole Minor Units, so a fraction of one is not a representable quantity.
_Avoid_: Cents, Smallest unit

**Reserved Amount**:
The portion of an Account's balance committed to Transfers that have not yet reached a terminal state. It is still held by the Account but cannot be spent again.
_Avoid_: Hold, Frozen funds, Pending balance

**Available Balance**:
What an Account can actually spend: its balance minus its Reserved Amount. This is the figure an overdraft check tests against.
_Avoid_: Spendable balance, Free balance

### Transfers and their lifecycle

**Transfer**:
A request to move an amount of Money from one Account to another, possibly across Currencies. It has a lifecycle: `PENDING` while its Checks are outstanding, then terminally `SETTLED`, `REJECTED` or `EXPIRED`.
_Avoid_: Payment, Utalás (Hungarian source term)

**Transaction**:
_Not an entity._ The label of the screen that lists Transfers in every state. A recorded Transfer is still a Transfer — this context has one word for it.
_Avoid_: using this as a name for a persisted or executed Transfer

**Settlement**:
The point at which a `PENDING` Transfer's money actually moves: the source Account's balance and Reserved Amount both fall, the destination Account's balance rises. Reserving funds at request time is not Settlement.
_Avoid_: Execution, Clearing, Completion

**Check**:
A condition a Transfer must satisfy before it can settle — fraud screening, manual approval — answered by a party outside this context. A human approver and an automated service are the same kind of thing here.
_Avoid_: Approval, Gate, Rule

**Check Ledger**:
The per-Transfer record of which Checks it requires and how each has been answered. It is what makes "why is this Transfer still pending" a question with an answer.
_Avoid_: Checklist, Approval log

**Verdict**:
A Check's answer for one Transfer: approved or rejected. A Transfer settles when every Check has approved and rejects the moment any one rejects.
_Avoid_: Result, Decision, Outcome

**Expiry**:
The terminal state of a `PENDING` Transfer whose Checks were not all answered before its deadline. It releases the Reserved Amount without moving money.
_Avoid_: Timeout, Cancellation

### Integration

**Exchange Rate**:
The rate used to convert Money from the source Account's Currency to the destination Account's, obtained from an external provider when the Transfer is requested and fixed for that Transfer's life. The provider is unreliable — it returns errors and responds slowly — so requesting a Transfer must tolerate that.
_Avoid_: Rate, FX rate

**Idempotency Key**:
A client-supplied value (sent as `X-Idempotency-Key`) that identifies a single Transfer *intent*, so that retrying the same request never moves money twice. It identifies what the user meant to do, not an individual HTTP attempt.
_Avoid_: Request ID, dedup key

**Outbox Event**:

1	# Deferred decisions
2	
3	Running list of things consciously left out, with the reasoning. Feeds the
4	README's TODO section, which the task grades as heavily as the code.
5	
6	Each entry: what was deferred, why, and what it would take to do properly.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Client retry semantics for `409 Conflict`
11	
12	**Deferred.** Two different situations return `409`, and a client must treat
13	them oppositely:
14	
15	- **Request in progress** — the same key and payload are already being
16	  processed. Retrying later is correct and expected.
17	- **Idempotency key reused with a different payload** — the client has made a
18	  mistake. Retrying will never succeed and must not be attempted.
19	
20	MVP returns `409` for both, with a distinct problem `type` URN so the two are
21	at least distinguishable programmatically, and `Retry-After` present on the
22	in-progress case only.
23	
24	**Why deferred:** the remaining work is largely a UX and client-contract
25	problem — how the frontend surfaces each case, whether it retries
26	automatically, what the user is told — rather than a backend correctness gap.
27	The backend already reports enough to tell them apart.
28	
29	**What it would take:** decide whether the payload-mismatch case deserves its
30	own status code (`422`) rather than sharing `409`; define client retry policy
31	(backoff for in-progress, hard stop for mismatch); surface both distinctly in
32	the React error handling.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## Authentication
37	
38	**Deferred.** No authentication scheme. Spring Security is wired with an
39	explicit, justified stateless filter chain that denies by default and permits
40	the public API by name, so nothing a caller reaches needs credentials.
41	
42	**Why deferred:** nothing in the functional or non-functional requirements
43	references a caller — transfers operate on bare account IDs, and all three
44	screens are unscoped. Building auth spends budget on something the task never
45	asks for.
46	
47	**What it would take, in order:** bearer token validation → ownership check on
48	the transfer source account → scoping the transactions list to the caller.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Account ownership (`User` / `Customer`)
53	
54	**Deferred.** `Account` is the atomic entity. No owner is modelled.
55	
56	**Why deferred:** no requirement queries, filters, or authorises by owner. An
57	owner entity with no behaviour is schema and test setup for nothing.
58	
59	**What it would take:** an `owner` field on the account record — additive and
60	non-breaking, since the response is a Java `record`.
61	
62	---
63	
64	## Idempotency keys are globally scoped
65	
66	**Deferred.** Keys live in one namespace shared by all callers.
67	
68	**Why deferred:** direct consequence of having no caller identity — there is
69	nothing to scope a key to.
70	
71	**Residual risk:** key-squatting. A caller who guesses a key before its
72	legitimate owner uses it claims it first, and the legitimate request gets
73	`409` and never executes. Denial of service on one transfer; no money moves
74	and nothing is disclosed. Mitigated in the MVP by requiring keys to be
75	well-formed UUIDs, making a guess a 122-bit problem.
76	
77	**What it would take:** a composite unique key of `(caller, idempotency_key)`
78	— which requires the caller identity deferred above.
79	
80	---

122	## 3. Idempotency lives in the service layer, behind a seam
123	
124	Not in the request pipeline. A filter-level check decides *before* the
125	transaction that moves money opens, leaving a window between "no prior request
126	found" and "funds reserved" — exactly the race the requirement is about. It
127	also fights the servlet API: hashing the body consumes the stream, and
128	replaying a `201` means re-emitting a response you didn't produce.
129	
130	The seam, so the implementation can be replaced without touching money
131	movement:
132	
133	```java
134	public interface IdempotentExecution {
135	    <T> T executeOnce(String key, String payloadHash, Supplier<T> operation);
136	}
137	```
138	
139	Named replacements it holds a place for: pessimistic `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
140	instead of relying on constraint violation, a Redis-backed store once there is
141	more than one instance, or folding into the outbox.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## 4. Request handling is three phases
146	
147	1. **Claim the key** — insert the idempotency row as `IN_PROGRESS`, commit
148	   immediately and alone. The unique constraint serialises concurrent
149	   duplicates.
150	2. **Resolve the FX rate** — no transaction open, no locks held. A flaky
151	   provider costs only wall clock.
152	3. **Reserve funds** — one transaction: lock both accounts, check the available
153	   balance, reserve, create the transfer and its check ledger, *and* flip the
154	   idempotency record to `SUCCEEDED` with the stored response.
155	
156	Phase 3 bundles the status update with the reservation deliberately. If they
157	could commit separately, a crash between them leaves funds reserved and the
158	record stuck at `IN_PROGRESS` — the client is told `409` forever for a transfer
159	that really happened. Bundled, the only crash window is after phase 1: a
160	claimed key with nothing reserved, which is a stale row and exactly what the
161	retry path exists for.
162	
163	---
164	
165	## 5. Duplicate resolution
166	
167	Resolved at the top of `executeOnce`, before the FX call, so a duplicate costs
168	nothing. The insert is the test; on constraint violation, read the row:
169	
170	| Existing status | Response |
171	|---|---|
172	| `IN_PROGRESS` | `409 Conflict` |
173	| `SUCCEEDED` | replay the stored `201` |
174	| `FAILED` | proceed and execute |
175	| key reused with a different payload | `409 Conflict`, distinct error code |
176	
177	Two traps:
178	
179	- **The `FAILED` path is itself a race.** Two retries both read `FAILED` and
180	  both proceed. Claim it with a conditional update —
181	  `UPDATE ... SET status='IN_PROGRESS' WHERE key=? AND status='FAILED'` — and
182	  check the affected-row count. Exactly one caller gets `1`; the loser gets
183	  `409`. The same conditional-update-plus-rows-affected pattern recurs for
184	  verdicts and for expiry.
185	- **Marking `FAILED` needs its own transaction.** A rollback would undo the
186	  status write too, stranding the row at `IN_PROGRESS` and making retry
187	  impossible. Use `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)`.
188	
189	Keys must be well-formed UUIDs (`400` otherwise). `FAILED` covers both business
190	rejections and infrastructure failures — both retryable. Since the request
191	returns once funds are reserved, this only governs reservation-time failures,
192	not transfer outcomes.
193	
194	The payload-mismatch case shares `409` with the in-progress case but carries a
195	distinct problem `type` URN (`urn:problem:request-in-progress` vs
196	`urn:problem:idempotency-key-reused`, see §18), because a client may retry the
197	first and must never retry the second.
198

201	## 6. Concurrency: pessimistic locks in a deterministic order
202	
203	`@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` on the account lookup, with accounts
204	always locked in **ascending ID order** rather than by their role in the
205	transfer. Opposing transfers then contend for the same lock first, so deadlock
206	is structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.
207	
208	Viable because §4 moved the FX call out of the transaction — the classic
209	objection to pessimistic locking is holding locks across slow work, and the
210	slow work was deliberately removed.
211	
212	The lock is taken *before* the balance check, or the balance read can be
213	invalidated before the reservation. Self-transfers (A→A) are rejected with
214	`422` before locking.
215	
216	**Rejected — optimistic locking (`@Version`).** Needs a bounded retry loop, and
217	retries hardest exactly when contention is worst.
218	
219	**Rejected — an application-level `reserved` flag on the account.** A database
220	lock is released automatically when a transaction ends, including on a dropped
221	connection; a flag is a row you wrote, so a crash between setting and clearing
222	freezes the account permanently, requiring a TTL and a reaper. Setting the flag
223	safely takes a row lock anyway, so it layers on the engine's locking rather
224	than replacing it. It converts an invisible ~50ms wait into a client-visible
225	`409`. And it does not fix deadlock — the same ordering rule is still needed.
226	
227	*A lock is infrastructure; a reservation is domain state.* If it outlives a
228	request and a human can see it, model it. If it only stops two concurrent
229	writes inside one request, that is what the database is for.

233	## 7. Transfers have an asynchronous lifecycle
234	
235	`PENDING` → `SETTLED` / `REJECTED` / `EXPIRED`. Funds are reserved at request
236	time; the money moves at settlement.

238	The reasoning, what it cost, and the rejected alternatives are in
239	[ADR-0001](adr/0001-asynchronous-transfer-lifecycle.md) — the one decision here

245	## 8. Orchestration, driven by a per-transfer check ledger
246	
247	The transfer service owns the state machine. At creation — *in the same
248	transaction as the transfer*, so a transfer can never exist without its
249	checklist — a policy writes one row per required check:
250	
251	| transfer_id | check | status |
252	|---|---|---|
253	| t-1 | `FRAUD` | `PENDING` |
254	| t-1 | `MANUAL_APPROVAL` | `PENDING` |
255	
256	Settles when no row is `PENDING` and none is `REJECTED`; rejects the moment any
257	row is `REJECTED`. A new check type is a policy line and a row.
258	
259	**Rejected — choreography.** With no central record of what a transfer waits
260	on, "why is this stuck" has no queryable answer and the frontend has nothing to
261	render. The ledger *is* the pending-state UI, the audit trail, and the test
262	seam.
263	
264	Verdicts must be idempotent — a check reporting `APPROVED` twice must not
265	advance anything twice. Same conditional update as §5.

319	## 12. Hand-rolled transactional outbox
320	
321	An event row is written in the same transaction as the transfer, so neither can
322	exist without the other. A `@Scheduled` poller publishes unsent rows through a
323	one-method `EventPublisher` interface and marks them sent. At-least-once;
324	consumers must tolerate duplicates, which they must anyway.
325	
326	**Kafka does not replace this.** "Commit to the database, then send to Kafka"
327	is still two writes with no transaction spanning them. Kafka is the transport
328	under `publish()`; the outbox is what makes the handoff atomic.
329	
330	Hand-rolled (~55 lines) rather than adopting Spring Modulith's Event
331	Publication Registry, because the outbox is one of the few places the task asks
332	for demonstrated architectural judgement and a dependency demonstrates less of
333	it than code you can defend. Modulith and Kafka are named in the README as the
334	production answers — see [deferred.md](deferred.md).
335	
336	In this build `publish()` writes a structured log line, and a profile-gated
337	`StubFraudDetection` consumes `CheckRequested` and reports a verdict a beat
338	later, so the async lifecycle is *visible* in the UI rather than taken on
339	faith. It can reject as well as approve, so the rejection path is demoable. It
340	is a fake consumer, not a fake mechanism — the outbox, ledger and verdict
341	endpoint it exercises are all real.

345	## 13. Balances: two fields on `Account`
346	
347	`balance` (what the account holds) and `reservedAmount` (committed to in-flight
348	transfers). Available = `balance - reservedAmount`, which is the overdraft
349	check under the lock from §6. Reserving increments `reservedAmount`; settling
350	decrements both; rejecting or expiring decrements only `reservedAmount`.
351	
352	This is the customer-facing model real banks present — "ledger balance" and
353	"available balance" are the industry terms, and a card authorization hold works
354	exactly this way.
355	
356	What banks run *underneath* is double-entry: balances are a materialized
357	projection over a posting log, with internal accounts (suspense, clearing, FX
358	position) absorbing cross-currency differences so each currency's books balance
359	independently. Deferred deliberately — see [deferred.md](deferred.md).

363	## 14. Unanswered checks expire
364	
365	Each check row carries a deadline. A `@Scheduled` reaper finds overdue
366	`PENDING` transfers, marks them `EXPIRED`, releases the reservation and
367	publishes the event.

369	Without it, a check that never responds leaves funds reserved forever with no
370	transaction to show for it — and `PENDING` would have no exit that does not
371	depend on an external service behaving. Cheap because the scheduled-poller
372	machinery already exists for the outbox.
373	
374	A verdict arriving *after* expiry must not settle the transfer. Same
375	conditional-update guard as §5.

379	## 15. The FX rate is locked at request time

381	Fetched during creation, stored on the transfer with its fetch timestamp, used
382	at settlement.

384	The argument is failure handling, not accuracy. Fetching at settlement means
385	the flaky provider is called *after* every check has approved — a 503 there
386	leaves an approved transfer that cannot settle, with no caller to tell and no
387	one to retry, requiring a settlement retry queue and a policy for permanently
388	unsettleable transfers. Locking at request keeps the failure in front of the
389	caller, which is the "handle the flaky API elegantly" requirement, and keeps
390	the call in the position §4 put it.
391	
392	Rate staleness on a long-pending transfer is already handled: **the quote's
393	validity window and the check deadline in §14 are the same clock.** A transfer
394	that outlives its quote expires and releases its funds. Whether to re-quote
395	instead is a business decision, not a technical one.

399	## 16. Money is a `long` count of minor units
400	
401	`record Money(long minorUnits, Currency currency)`, as a JPA `@Embeddable` —
402	one record flattens to two columns. Amounts are counted in fillér and cents,
403	never in forints and euros.
404	
405	**Rejected — `BigDecimal`.** The usual argument against it (float drift) does
406	not apply: `BigDecimal` is exact. The real problem is that it is
407	**unconstrained**. Nothing stops a mis-scaled column or a careless division
408	producing `100.505` HUF — a quantity that cannot exist. `long` fillér makes the
409	sub-unit *unrepresentable* rather than merely discouraged, and it leaves
410	exactly one place in the codebase where rounding happens.
411	
412	It also removes a trap with no TypeScript equivalent: **`BigDecimal.equals`
413	compares scale**, so `new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00"))` is
414	`false` while `compareTo` says they are equal. Two amounts that are the same
415	money fail an equality assertion, and a `record`'s generated `equals` inherits
416	the problem.
417	
418	- **Wire format is an integer count of minor units, in a field named
419	  `amountMinor`.** The name is the mitigation: `"amount": 10050` invites
420	  someone to read 10050 forints, `"amountMinor": 10050` does not.
421	- **Per-currency decimals (EUR/USD 2, HUF 0) live only at the edges** — form
422	  parsing and display. The core never divides by 100.
423	- **The rate stays `BigDecimal`.** It is the one value that is genuinely a
424	  decimal, and it is never money.
425	- `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN`, and **`422` when a converted amount rounds to
426	  zero** — 1 HUF to EUR would otherwise debit the source and credit nothing.
427	
428	The single conversion, and the most error-prone line in the backend:
429	
430	```
431	destMinor = round(srcMinor × rate × 10^(destScale − srcScale))
432	```
433	
434	e.g. `10050 × 390.12 × 10^(0−2) = 39207.06 → 39207 Ft`. Table-test it: EUR→HUF,
435	HUF→EUR, USD→EUR, same-currency (no provider call at all), and round-to-zero.
436	
437	**Honest consequence: money is not conserved across the two accounts.** The
438	rounding remainder vanishes. That is what the double-entry deferral costs — see
439	[deferred.md](deferred.md).
440	
441	**Verify in the first hour:** Hibernate's support for `record` types as
442	`@Embeddable`. It has been supported since Hibernate 6.2 and Boot 4 ships
443	Hibernate 7, but a wrong assumption here re-shapes every entity.

594	Retry policy must be narrowed: `retry: (n, err) => n < 3 && err.status >= 500`.
595	Query's default retries anything — retrying a `422` is noise, and a `409
596	REQUEST_IN_PROGRESS` should wait for its `Retry-After` (§18), not Query's
597	backoff.
598	
599	---
600	
601	## 22. TanStack Form + zod, and no global state library
602	
603	**No Redux, Zustand or Jotai.** Once Query owns server state and the router owns
604	route state, there is no client state left to manage. The README answer is *"I
605	didn't add one, because there was nothing left to manage"*; if one were ever
606	needed, the escalation is Context + `useReducer` before a library.
607	
608	**Form: TanStack Form** (over react-hook-form — provider consistency), with zod
609	for the schema. zod is still needed, and how the two connect has changed:
610	
611	- TanStack Form has **no schema language of its own**; as of v1 it speaks
612	  **Standard Schema** natively. `@tanstack/zod-form-adapter` and `zodValidator`
613	  are **gone** — pass the schema straight in as
614	  `validators: { onChange: schema }`. Requires zod ≥ 3.24.
615	- **Transforms do not flow through.** The docs are explicit: *"Validation will
616	  not provide you with transformed values."* `onSubmit` receives **input**-typed
617	  data, so getting the output type means calling `schema.parse(value)` inside
618	  `onSubmit`. The property worth keeping — the schema owns the
619	  decimal → minor-unit conversion — survives as one explicit line.
620	- `z.input` vs `z.output` is the confusing part (`z.infer` aliases *output*).
621	  Worth a comment where it bites.
622	- **Cross-field rules go in the form-level validator**, which can set errors on
623	  several fields at once. The self-transfer check lives there, caught in the
624	  browser before §6's `422`.
625	- Known friction: a form-level zod `onChange` validator over-renders
626	  (TanStack/form#1625). Irrelevant at four fields.
627	
628	**Currency is not a form field.** The amount is *always* denominated in the
629	source account's currency, so the payload is
630	`{ fromAccountId, toAccountId, amountMinor }` plus `X-Idempotency-Key`, and the
631	server derives the currency from the source account. That deletes a whole bug
632	class — a client claiming EUR on a HUF account cannot be expressed.
633	
634	The zod schema is therefore a **factory over the accounts list**,
635	`makeTransferSchema(accounts)`, so the decimal-scale rule derives from the
636	selected source account. Because the form-level validator re-runs on any field
637	change, switching the source account from EUR to HUF immediately re-invalidates
638	`"100.50"` with no manual dependency wiring. The UI shows the currency as an
639	adornment on the input.
640	
641	Sources: `tanstack.com/form/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/validation` and
642	`.../submission-handling`.
643	
644	---
645	
646	## 23. Bootstrap 5, CSS only, plus CSS Modules
647	
648	**Rejected — shadcn/ui, MUI, Mantine** (overkill for four screens) **and
649	no library at all** (underkill — hand-rolled CSS at this size looks like a
650	corner cut).
651	
652	The specific reason a component library's value is unused here: **this app has
653	no JavaScript-driven components.** There is no dialog, combobox, popover or
654	dropdown menu. A `<select>`, a form, a table, a badge and a spinner are native
655	elements or pure CSS. Radix's entire proposition — managed focus, roving
656	tabindex, portal rendering — buys nothing on this screen list, which is also the
657	README justification.
658	
659	- **No `react-bootstrap` and no Bootstrap JS bundle** — a single CSS import.
660	  The reflex is to reach for the React wrapper, which reintroduces exactly the
661	  weight this choice avoids.
662	- CSS Modules need no Vite configuration.
663	- `.is-invalid` / `.invalid-feedback` map directly onto TanStack Form's error
664	  state.
665	- The dated look is about ten lines of Bootstrap 5.3 CSS custom properties
666	  (`--bs-primary` and friends); `data-bs-theme="dark"` is built in.
667	
668	---
669	
670	## 24. Frontend testing: extract logic, unit test it, Playwright end-to-mock
671	
672	The rule: **pull logic out into pure TypeScript modules and unit test those;
673	write as few React integration tests as possible.** Integration confidence comes
674	from the browser, not from jsdom.
675	
676	Extraction list — `money.ts`, `transferSchema.ts`, `problem.ts`,
677	`idempotency.ts`, `events.ts`. Applying the rule turns the three tests that
678	matter most into unit tests:
679	
680	- **Idempotency key lifecycle** → a plain module, no React.
681	- **`ProblemDetail` handling** → `problemToMessage(problem): { title, body,
682	  retryable }`, a pure table test.
683	- **SSE handling** → `invalidationsFor(event): QueryKey[]` is pure; React only
684	  does `keys.forEach(k => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: k }))`. **This makes
685	  the SSE yak-shave disappear**: no jsdom `EventSource` polyfill, no MSW
686	  streaming, no flake.
687	
688	Stack: **Vitest + React Testing Library**. Vitest over Jest because Vite is
689	already there — same config, same transform pipeline, no second toolchain. **MSW
690	probably drops entirely**: Playwright owns network mocking, and the surviving
691	RTL tests ("does this field show its error") touch no network.
692	
693	**The idempotency-key rule, which is the frontend half of a graded
694	requirement:** the key identifies a **user intent**, not an HTTP attempt.
695	Generate it once when the form becomes ready, hold it in a ref, and reset it
696	only after a success. Generating it inside `mutationFn` defeats the entire
697	mechanism — every retry gets a fresh key and the server sees a new transfer.
698	
699	**Playwright is end-to-mock, not true E2E.** A real browser — real
700	`EventSource`, real focus and blur, real navigation — against a deterministic
701	scripted backend. Mock with **`page.route()`, not MSW-in-browser**: no service
702	worker, no extra build mode, and the mocks live in the spec that depends on them.
703	
704	**`route.fulfill()` takes `string | Buffer` only — there is no streaming body**
705	(Playwright #33564 is the open request; #15353 is the SSE question). So an SSE
706	event cannot be pushed mid-test, which is exactly what asserting
707	`PENDING → SETTLED` needs. Instead **stub `window.EventSource` via
708	`addInitScript`**, which runs before app code:
709	
710	1. assert the row reads Pending
711	2. `page.route` the transfer endpoint to return the settled version — *truth
712	   changes*
713	3. `page.evaluate` dispatches a `MessageEvent` on the fake source
714	4. assert the row reads Settled
715	
716	That drives §17's design end to end — thin event → invalidate → refetch →
717	render — deterministically, with no `waitForTimeout`. True E2E goes to
718	[deferred.md](deferred.md) with its gap named.
719	
720	---
721	
722	## 25. Backend tests run on H2
723	
724	**Rejected — Testcontainers.** Test what you ship: the task blesses H2 and the
725	app runs on H2. And Testcontainers needs Docker running on the reviewer's
726	machine — `./mvnw test` failing for that reason is a bad first impression bought
727	very cheaply. Since Playwright is end-to-mock (§24), nothing outside the JVM
728	needs a realistic database either.
729	
730	Setup cost is one test-scoped dependency (`com.h2database:h2`); Spring Boot
731	auto-configures an in-memory database from there. No Docker, no container, no
732	port.
733	
734	**The Spring testing landscape**, because which annotation you reach for *is*
735	the design decision:
736	
737	| Layer | What Spring starts | DB? | ~boot |
738	|---|---|---|---|
739	| plain JUnit | nothing | no | 0 ms |
740	| `@WebMvcTest` | controllers, JSON, validation, exception handlers, security | no | 1–2 s |
741	| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA + in-memory DB, no web | yes | ~2 s |
742	| `@SpringBootTest` | everything | yes | 3–8 s |
743	
744	- "Contract test the API interface" is `@WebMvcTest`, and §26 pins that contract
745	  from both ends.
746	- "Unit test the logic" is really a **design** instruction: `decide(List<CheckRow>)
747	  → Settle | Reject | Wait` is testable; the same logic inside a `@Service` that
748	  also does I/O is not. Same move as §24's extraction list.
749	- **What unit tests cannot reach is where this project's difficulty lives.**
750	  "The unique constraint serialises concurrent duplicates" (§4),
751	  "ascending-ID locking makes deadlock structurally impossible" (§6),
752	  "`UPDATE … WHERE status='FAILED'` returns 1 for exactly one caller" (§5) are
753	  claims about the *database*, as is every transaction boundary in the async
754	  lifecycle. *Konkurencia és adatintegritás* is a named graded requirement, so
755	  these are the tests that count.
756	
757	**Boot 4 moved the furniture** (found while writing ticket 01's tests, recorded
758	here because every tutorial and every model's training data predates it):
759	
760	- **`TestRestTemplate` no longer exists.** The replacement is Spring Framework
761	  7's `RestTestClient`, used as
762	  `RestTestClient.bindToServer().baseUrl("http://localhost:" + port).build()`
763	  with a fluent `.expectStatus()` / `.jsonPath()` API. Reach for it in any
764	  `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`.
765	- **The slice annotations changed packages**, and the compiler error for these
766	  is an unhelpful "cannot find symbol":
767	  `@DataJpaTest` → `org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure`,
768	  `TestEntityManager` → `org.springframework.boot.jpa.test.autoconfigure`,
769	  `@EntityScan` → `org.springframework.boot.persistence.autoconfigure`.
770	- **Starters were split by slice.** It is `spring-boot-starter-webmvc`, not
771	  `spring-boot-starter-web`, and test support arrives as one `*-test` starter
772	  per slice (`spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test`, `-data-jpa-test`, …) rather than
773	  a single `spring-boot-starter-test`.
774	- **`TestEntityManager` does not resolve as a constructor parameter** —
775	  `ParameterResolutionException` at runtime, not a compile error. Use
776	  `@Autowired` field injection.
777	
778	One trap that is not Boot 4's fault but shows up the moment tests need their own
779	`@Entity` or `@RestController`: **test sources share the runtime classpath with
780	main sources**, so anything annotated under `hu.bankmonitor.payments` in
781	`src/test` is component-scanned into *every* `@SpringBootTest` in the suite.
782	Ticket 01 keeps its throwaway entity and probe controller in
783	`hu.bankmonitor.testsupport` — deliberately outside the scan root — and
784	`@Import`s or `@EntityScan`s them explicitly. This gets sharper from ticket 02:
785	once Flyway owns the schema and `ddl-auto=validate` is on, one leaked test entity
786	with no migration behind it fails startup for every database test there is.
787	
788	**Three traps:**
789	
790	- **Context caching.** `@SpringBootTest` boots the application context once and
791	  reuses it — but every distinct combination of `@MockitoBean`,
792	  `@ActiveProfiles` and `@TestPropertySource` creates a *separate* cached
793	  context. Careless variation turns one five-second boot into eight.
794	- **`@Transactional` on a concurrency test method silently defeats it.** Spring
795	  runs the test in a single transaction, so the second thread cannot see the
796	  first thread's uncommitted claim; both "succeed" and the test passes while
797	  proving nothing. Write it non-transactional with manual cleanup.
798	- **Line the threads up with a `CountDownLatch`** on
799	  `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`. Without it, thread one finishes
800	  before thread two starts and the race never happens. Assert **exactly** one
801	  `201` and one `409`.
802	
803	Realistic suite, 15–20 tests:
804	
805	- **unit** — money conversion, reject-on-zero, check policy, ledger decision
806	- **`@WebMvcTest`** — status codes, `ProblemDetail` URNs, missing and malformed
807	  idempotency keys, validation bodies
808	- **`@DataJpaTest`** — the idempotency unique constraint, conditional-update
809	  rows-affected, the pessimistic-lock query
810	- **`@SpringBootTest`** — concurrent same-key requests yield exactly one `201`;
811	  opposing transfers do not deadlock; full lifecycle create → outbox → verdict →
812	  `SETTLED`; FX provider fails twice then succeeds
813	
814	H2's behaviour is close enough for these to be meaningful, but not identical to
815	Postgres — see [deferred.md](deferred.md).
816	
817	---
818	
819	## 26. Frontend API types are generated from OpenAPI
820	
821	`springdoc-openapi` exposes `/v3/api-docs`; `openapi-typescript` generates a
822	`.d.ts` the frontend imports.
823	
824	This is the only thing standing between end-to-mock tests (§24) and
825	self-congratulation: **it converts mock drift into a compile error.** A
826	Playwright mock returning a shape the backend no longer produces stops being a
827	green test and starts being a failed build. It also puts §18's problem-type URNs
828	in exactly one place.
829	
830	Caveats: the generated file is checked in and regenerated by hand, so it needs a
831	CI check or at minimum a README line — otherwise it goes stale, which is its own
832	[deferred.md](deferred.md) entry. **Verify springdoc's Spring Boot 4 support in
833	the first hour**, alongside §16's Hibernate question. Both are "has the
834	ecosystem caught up to Boot 4" bets: cheap to check now, expensive to discover
835	late.
836	
837	---
838	
839	## 27. The flaky FX provider: timeouts, retry, then fail to the caller
840	
841	No cache, no circuit breaker. Timeouts on the `RestClient`, `@Retryable` around
842	the call, and on exhaustion a `503` with
843	`urn:problem:fx-provider-unavailable` and a `Retry-After`.
844	
845	`@Retryable` is **built into Spring Framework 7**, so Boot 4 needs neither
846	`spring-retry` nor Resilience4j. Two migration details that every tutorial
847	predates: the enabling annotation is **`@EnableResilientMethods`** (not
848	`@EnableRetry`), and `maxAttempts` was renamed **`maxRetries`**.
849	
850	- **Timeouts are non-negotiable.** Without them "responds slowly" is unbounded,
851	  and a virtual thread parks forever while holding an `IN_PROGRESS` idempotency
852	  claim — the flaky provider becomes a stuck transfer.
853	- Retry `5xx` and timeouts. **Never retry `4xx`.**
854	
855	**Why the lean version is complete, rather than a corner cut:** §5 marks the
856	idempotency record `FAILED`, which is explicitly retryable, so the client
857	resubmits with the *same key* and the server executes properly. Failing to the
858	caller is not giving up — it hands the retry to the layer that already has
859	idempotency making it safe. §5, §15 and §21's retry policy cohere into one
860	answer to the "handle the flaky API elegantly" requirement.
861	
862	**Rejected — a circuit breaker.** A breaker exists to protect a scarce thread
863	pool from being consumed by calls that will fail. Virtual threads mean threads
864	are not scarce, and the retry budget is already bounded by the timeout. Goes to
865	[deferred.md](deferred.md).
866	
867	**Rejected — caching rates.** A legitimate want, declined on scope. If it comes
868	back: §15 already stores the fetch timestamp on the transfer, so a cached rate
869	stays auditable.
870	
871	**Free win:** Spring Framework 7 publishes `MethodRetryEvent`, observable with
872	`@EventListener`. A test can **assert that the retry actually happened** without
873	mocking framework internals — resilience tested rather than claimed, on a graded
874	line.
875	
876	Sources: `danvega.dev/blog/spring-boot-4-native-retry-support`; the `@Retryable`
877	javadoc; the Moderne spring-retry → Framework 7 migration recipe.
878	
879	---
880	
881	## 28. The mock FX provider is a real HTTP endpoint inside the app
882	
883	`@Profile("mock-fx")`, e.g. `GET /mock/fx/rates?base=EUR&quote=HUF`, called over
884	real HTTP by the real client. The client reads `fx.base-url` from configuration,
885	so swapping in a real provider is a property change.
886	
887	**Rejected — a stub `@Bean` implementing the provider interface.** It puts the
888	failure simulation *above* the HTTP client, so none of §27's timeouts, retries
889	or error mapping are ever exercised. The thing being demonstrated would be the
890	thing being mocked out.
891	
892	**Rejected — WireMock as a separate server.** Friction for the reviewer, for a
893	capability the in-process endpoint already provides. In tests, Spring's
894	**`MockRestServiceServer`** covers it with no new dependency — it binds to
895	`RestClient.builder()` and scripts `503, 503, 200` cleanly. It sits *above* the
896	transport, though, so it **cannot exercise the read timeout** →
897	[deferred.md](deferred.md).
898	
899	**It must stay out of the application's cross-cutting layers**, or it stops
900	being a believable third party. Five distinct Spring mechanisms, each doing one
901	job:
902	
903	- **Security: total bypass, not `permitAll`** — a `WebSecurityCustomizer` with
904	  `web.ignoring().requestMatchers("/mock/**")`. Spring's docs discourage
905	  `ignoring()` for real endpoints because it forgoes security headers; here that
906	  is exactly the point.
907	- **`@RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "…payments.api")`**, scoped rather
908	  than global — otherwise a "third-party service" emits *our* `ProblemDetail`
909	  shape and the fiction collapses.
910	- **`FilterRegistrationBean` with `addUrlPatterns("/api/*", "/internal/*")`** so
911	  logging and MDC filters never touch it.
912	- Out of the `CorsConfigurationSource` mapping entirely — it is
913	  server-to-server.
914	- Its own package, `…payments.mockfx`, depending on nothing in the domain (§30).
915	
916	**Trap this creates:** the application now calls itself over HTTP. On Tomcat's
917	classic thread pool that can deadlock under load — the inbound request holds a
918	thread while waiting for a second one to serve its own outbound call. **This
919	makes `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` load-bearing rather than a
920	nicety**, and it is worth one README sentence saying why.
921	
922	---
923	
924	## 29. Maven, Flyway, and `ddl-auto=validate`
925	
926	**Maven**, the Initializr default. `./mvnw` means the reviewer installs nothing
927	and `pom.xml` is readable by any Java developer; Gradle's incremental-build edge
928	is irrelevant at this size, and §20's two-process setup means there is no
929	frontend plugin, no Node download and no build profile to justify it.
930	
931	**Flyway with `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate`**, not `create-drop`.
932	Partly signalling — `ddl-auto` generating schema anywhere but a throwaway
933	database is a known foot-gun — but the substantive reason is that the migration
934	directory shows every table, type, constraint and index as SQL, instead of a
935	schema reconstructed by reading annotations across six entity classes. It is
936	also the natural home for the indexes the design implies: the outbox poller's
937	`WHERE sent_at IS NULL`, the reaper's
938	`WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND deadline < ?`.
939	
940	**One migration per slice, not one file up front** (amended when the work was
941	broken into tickets). The original decision was a single `V1__init.sql` carrying
942	the whole schema from the first commit, on the grounds that one file reads
943	better than six. That would have meant writing the outbox, check-ledger and
944	idempotency tables before those entities existed — schema written against a
945	design rather than against code, and the one artefact that can no longer be
946	checked by `validate` while it is being written. Each slice now ships the
947	migration for the table it introduces (`V1__accounts.sql`,
948	`V2__transfers.sql`, …), including the later ones that only add a column. What
949	made the original decision worth keeping — `validate` on from the very first
950	commit — is unaffected, and is the part that actually catches mismatches.
951	
952	**From day one, not baselined at the end.** Hibernate's implicit naming strategy
953	silently maps `fromAccountId` to `from_account_id`, and a `Money` embeddable to
954	`amount_minor_units` / `amount_currency`. With `validate` on from the first
955	commit, each mismatch fails at startup naming the exact column; discovered at
956	the end, they arrive all at once.
957	
958	**Column *types* are the sharper half of that, and ticket 01's spike found one
959	that would otherwise have cost an afternoon.** `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` on
960	Hibernate 7 / H2 does **not** produce a `varchar`. It emits a **native H2 `ENUM`**:
961	
962	```sql
963	create table spike_embeddable_host (
964	    id bigint generated by default as identity,
965	    minor_units bigint,
966	    currency enum ('EUR','HUF','USD'),   /* not varchar(3) */
967	    primary key (id)
968	)
969	```
970	
971	A migration writing `currency varchar(3)` — which looks obviously right, and
972	matches every tutorial written before Hibernate 6.2 — therefore fails `validate`
973	at startup. There are two ways out, and the choice belongs in the entity rather
974	than in the migration: write `enum (...)` in the migration and accept an
975	H2-specific column type, or pin the mapping with
976	`@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.VARCHAR)` on the component and write `varchar`.
977	
978	**Prefer the second.** The TODO list already marks verifying this schema against
979	Postgres as a production prerequisite, and a native H2 enum is exactly the kind
980	of thing that will not survive that move.
981	`RecordAsEmbeddableSpikeTest.mapsEnumComponentToNativeEnumColumn` asserts the
982	current behaviour, so changing it later is a visible decision rather than a
983	silent drift.
984	
985	**Seed data is not schema.** Demo accounts belong in a `@Profile("dev")`
986	`CommandLineRunner`, never in a migration — a Flyway seed runs in the test
987	suite too.
988	
989	**The dependency is `spring-boot-flyway`, not `flyway-core`.** Boot 4 split
990	auto-configuration out of `spring-boot-autoconfigure` into one module per
991	technology, so the coordinates every pre-Boot-4 answer gives you put the Flyway
992	library on the classpath with nothing to run it. The failure has no error and no
993	warning: the application starts, `ddl-auto=validate` passes against an empty
994	schema, and the first migration silently never runs.
995	`FlywayOwnsTheSchemaTest.flywayRunsAtStartup` asks the database for the schema
996	history table rather than trusting that the dependency implies the behaviour,
997	which is what caught it.
998	
999	---
1000	
1001	## 30. Package-by-feature
1002	
1003	```
1004	hu.bankmonitor.payments
1005	├── accounts/      Account, AccountController · repository package-private
1006	├── transfers/     Transfer, TransferController, TransferService
1007	│   └── checks/    CheckLedger, CheckPolicy, VerdictController (/internal)
1008	├── idempotency/   IdempotentExecution (public) · JDBC impl package-private
1009	├── fx/            ExchangeRateProvider (public) · HTTP client package-private
1010	├── outbox/        EventPublisher (public) · OutboxPoller package-private
1011	├── mockfx/        the §28 stand-in — depends on nothing
1012	└── common/        Money, Currency, problem-type constants
1013	```
1014	
1015	Dependencies run one way: `transfers` → `accounts`, `fx`, `idempotency`,
1016	`outbox`. Nothing points back. The three public ports are exactly §3, §11/§12
1017	and the FX client — hexagonal's value at the three places that asked for it,
1018	without the ceremony everywhere else.
1019	
1020	**The Java mechanism that makes this more than folder tidying, and which has no
1021	TypeScript equivalent:** Java's *default* access level is package-private, and
1022	it is compiler-enforced. A `TransferRepository` declared with no modifier is
1023	literally uncallable from outside `transfers/`. The boundary is not a lint rule
1024	or a convention — crossing it does not compile.
1025	
1026	**Rejected — package-by-layer.** It makes the layer the only boundary, so "where
1027	are your seams" answers "between controller and service", which is true of every
1028	Spring application ever written.
1029	
1030	**Rejected — hexagonal architecture.** A domain model, a JPA entity and a mapper
1031	for every concept, buying isolation from a database we are not going to swap.
1032	
1033	**Recommended, ~10 lines:** ArchUnit — `slices()…should().beFreeOfCycles()` plus
1034	"no controller may reference a repository". It turns "I drew boundaries" into a
1035	test that fails when someone crosses one. Spring Modulith would also do this,
1036	but §12 declined it and reintroducing it for verification alone would read as
1037	inconsistent.
1038	
1039	**Trap:** `@Transactional` on a non-public method is **silently ignored** under
1040	proxy-based AOP — no error, no warning, no transaction, and §4's phase-three
1041	atomicity quietly stops existing. Spring 6 relaxed this for CGLIB proxies, but
1042	the failure mode is silent either way. Rule: the **class** may be
1043	package-private; the **`@Transactional` method** stays public.
1044	
1045	---
1046	
1047	## 31. Residual API decisions
1048	
1049	- **No API versioning.** No `/v1` prefix → [deferred.md](deferred.md).
1050	- **No pagination.** All queries return everything →
1051	  [deferred.md](deferred.md).
1052	- **Account creation:** `POST /api/accounts` takes a currency and an initial
1053	  balance. **Currency is immutable thereafter** — an account that could change
1054	  denomination would make every historical balance ambiguous.
1055	- **Observability:** the Actuator health endpoint, plus §12's structured log
1056	  line on publish. Nothing else.
1057

# Design decisions

Settled in a grilling session on 2026-09-05, before any code was written.
Source material for the README's architecture section. Deferrals live in
[deferred.md](deferred.md); domain vocabulary in [../CONTEXT.md](../CONTEXT.md).

Each entry: what was decided, why, and what was rejected.
[ADR-0001](adr/0001-asynchronous-transfer-lifecycle.md) records the one decision
that shapes all the others.

## 1. `Account` is the atomic entity — no `User`

No owner is modelled. Every operational requirement is account-shaped:
transfers move money between account IDs, and all three screens are unscoped.
The spec's "felhasználói számla" reads as an adjective, not a modelling
instruction.

`Account` is a Java `record`, so adding an `owner` field later is additive and
non-breaking. `User` is named in `CONTEXT.md` as deliberately unmodelled.

**Rejected — an empty `interface AccountOwner {}` stub.** Works in TypeScript,
where structural typing makes an empty interface a maximally-wide "shape TBD"
placeholder that erases at compile time. Java is nominally typed, so an empty
interface nothing implements is satisfied by *nothing*; the field can only ever
be `null`; JPA cannot map a relationship to a type without an `@Id`, so the app
fails to start; and the field leaks into the API response as a permanent
`"owner": null`.

**Rejected — an `OwnershipPolicy` seam.** A stub that names a rule asserts the
rule exists. It would read as ownership implemented permissively, not deferred.

## 2. Authentication is stubbed, not built

No authentication scheme and no principal — nothing downstream learns who
called, so no controller signature carries identity.

Implemented with Spring Security rather than a hand-rolled filter, with each
setting justified rather than arbitrarily disabled: CSRF off (stateless JSON

server is a different origin), `permitAll` on `/api/**` — plus the one real
rule from §10.

**Watch out:** Spring Security runs before Spring MVC and intercepts CORS
preflight `OPTIONS` requests. Needs `.cors(withDefaults())` *and* a
`CorsConfigurationSource` bean; the MVC-level `@CrossOrigin` annotation alone
will not work. Symptom is opaque CORS failures in the browser while `curl`
works.

**Built in ticket 04, deny-by-default rather than permit-by-default.**
`anyRequest().denyAll()`, with `/api/**`, `/actuator/health` and the springdoc
paths named above it. The permissive version — `anyRequest().permitAll()` — is
the same thing for today's application and a different thing for tomorrow's:
under it, ticket 21's `/internal/**` prefix is reachable from the moment the
controller is written and stays reachable if its rule is ever removed, while
under this one it is unreachable until an entry exists. Deny-by-default is also
what makes the permits worth reading, since each one is a path someone chose to
open. `SecurityChainTest` asserts effects a caller can see — a status code, a
missing `Set-Cookie` — because a test asserting `csrf().disable()` was called
would only restate the source file.

A denial's body is currently empty rather than an §18 problem document, which
does not matter while nothing is denied on purpose. It becomes ticket 21's to
answer, when `/internal/**` produces the first refusal a caller is meant to
read.

**Rejected — `WebSecurityCustomizer.ignoring()` on `/api/**`.** It is the total
bypass §28 uses for the mock provider, and here it would forgo the security
response headers as well as the authorization rule. A permitted request still
passes through the chain; an ignored one is not a decision, it is an absence.

**Rejected — leaving `UserDetailsServiceAutoConfiguration` in place.** The
starter generates an in-memory account with a random password and prints it at
every startup under a warning to replace the configuration before production.
Harmless, since nothing authenticates — and precisely the "unfinished, not
decided" reading this section exists to avoid, printed in the reviewer's console
at every boot. Excluded on the application class.

**Rejected — omitting CORS on the grounds that §20's dev proxy makes the
frontend same-origin.** True for proxied calls and false for every other caller:
Swagger UI, a second frontend origin, any deployment that does not proxy. The

as wrong.

The README carries the settings themselves and the two traps they avoid, since
that is what a maintainer inherits. Both traps fail quietly rather than loudly,
which is the only reason they are worth a paragraph anywhere: the `ERROR`
dispatch one returns a plausible wrong status rather than an error, and the

## 3. Idempotency lives in the service layer, behind a seam

Not in the request pipeline. A filter-level check decides *before* the
transaction that moves money opens, leaving a window between "no prior request
found" and "funds reserved" — exactly the race the requirement is about. It
also fights the servlet API: hashing the body consumes the stream, and
replaying a `201` means re-emitting a response you didn't produce.

The seam, so the implementation can be replaced without touching money
movement:

```java
public interface IdempotentExecution {
    <T> T executeOnce(String key, String payloadHash, Supplier<T> operation);
}
```

Named replacements it holds a place for: pessimistic `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
instead of relying on constraint violation, a Redis-backed store once there is
more than one instance, or folding into the outbox.

## 4. Request handling is three phases

1. **Claim the key** — insert the idempotency row as `IN_PROGRESS`, commit
   immediately and alone. The unique constraint serialises concurrent
   duplicates.
2. **Resolve the FX rate** — no transaction open, no locks held. A flaky
   provider costs only wall clock.
3. **Reserve funds** — one transaction: lock both accounts, check the available
   balance, reserve, create the transfer and its check ledger, *and* flip the
   idempotency record to `SUCCEEDED` with the stored response.

Phase 3 bundles the status update with the reservation deliberately. If they
could commit separately, a crash between them leaves funds reserved and the
record stuck at `IN_PROGRESS` — the client is told `409` forever for a transfer
that really happened. Bundled, the only crash window is after phase 1: a
claimed key with nothing reserved, which is a stale row and exactly what the
retry path exists for.

---

## 5. Duplicate resolution

Resolved at the top of `executeOnce`, before the FX call, so a duplicate costs
nothing. The insert is the test; on constraint violation, read the row:

| Existing status | Response |
|---|---|
| `IN_PROGRESS` | `409 Conflict` |
| `SUCCEEDED` | replay the stored `201` |
| `FAILED` | proceed and execute |
| key reused with a different payload | `409 Conflict`, distinct error code |

Two traps:

- **The `FAILED` path is itself a race.** Two retries both read `FAILED` and
  both proceed. Claim it with a conditional update —
  `UPDATE ... SET status='IN_PROGRESS' WHERE key=? AND status='FAILED'` — and
  check the affected-row count. Exactly one caller gets `1`; the loser gets
  `409`. The same conditional-update-plus-rows-affected pattern recurs for
  verdicts and for expiry.
- **Marking `FAILED` needs its own transaction.** A rollback would undo the
  status write too, stranding the row at `IN_PROGRESS` and making retry
  impossible. Use `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)`.

Keys must be well-formed UUIDs (`400` otherwise). `FAILED` covers both business
rejections and infrastructure failures — both retryable. Since the request
returns once funds are reserved, this only governs reservation-time failures,
not transfer outcomes.

The payload-mismatch case shares `409` with the in-progress case but carries a
distinct problem `type` URN (`urn:problem:request-in-progress` vs
`urn:problem:idempotency-key-reused`, see §18), because a client may retry the
first and must never retry the second.

## 6. Concurrency: pessimistic locks in a deterministic order

`@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` on the account lookup, with accounts
always locked in **ascending ID order** rather than by their role in the
transfer. Opposing transfers then contend for the same lock first, so deadlock
is structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Viable because §4 moved the FX call out of the transaction — the classic
objection to pessimistic locking is holding locks across slow work, and the
slow work was deliberately removed.

The lock is taken *before* the balance check, or the balance read can be
invalidated before the reservation. Self-transfers (A→A) are rejected with
`422` before locking.

**Rejected — optimistic locking (`@Version`).** Needs a bounded retry loop, and
retries hardest exactly when contention is worst.

**Rejected — an application-level `reserved` flag on the account.** A database
lock is released automatically when a transaction ends, including on a dropped
connection; a flag is a row you wrote, so a crash between setting and clearing
freezes the account permanently, requiring a TTL and a reaper. Setting the flag
safely takes a row lock anyway, so it layers on the engine's locking rather
than replacing it. It converts an invisible ~50ms wait into a client-visible
`409`. And it does not fix deadlock — the same ordering rule is still needed.

*A lock is infrastructure; a reservation is domain state.* If it outlives a
request and a human can see it, model it. If it only stops two concurrent
writes inside one request, that is what the database is for.

## 7. Transfers have an asynchronous lifecycle

`PENDING` → `SETTLED` / `REJECTED` / `EXPIRED`. Funds are reserved at request
time; the money moves at settlement.

The reasoning, what it cost, and the rejected alternatives are in
[ADR-0001](adr/0001-asynchronous-transfer-lifecycle.md) — the one decision here
a fresh reader would otherwise "simplify" back to synchronous. Sections 8–15
below are its mechanics.

---

## 8. Orchestration, driven by a per-transfer check ledger

The transfer service owns the state machine. At creation — *in the same
transaction as the transfer*, so a transfer can never exist without its
checklist — a policy writes one row per required check:

| transfer_id | check | status |
|---|---|---|
| t-1 | `FRAUD` | `PENDING` |
| t-1 | `MANUAL_APPROVAL` | `PENDING` |

Settles when no row is `PENDING` and none is `REJECTED`; rejects the moment any
row is `REJECTED`. A new check type is a policy line and a row.

**Rejected — choreography.** With no central record of what a transfer waits
on, "why is this stuck" has no queryable answer and the frontend has nothing to
render. The ledger *is* the pending-state UI, the audit trail, and the test
seam.

Verdicts must be idempotent — a check reporting `APPROVED` twice must not
advance anything twice. Same conditional update as §5.

## 9. Verdicts arrive by inbound HTTP callback

`POST /internal/transfers/{id}/checks/{check}`, as a thin adapter over a
`recordVerdict(transferId, check, outcome)` domain operation. Tests drive the
operation directly; a broker consumer would be a second adapter over the same
operation.

The asymmetry with outbound events is deliberate, not accidental: outbound
needs an outbox because *we* own the atomicity of "the transfer committed,
therefore the event exists." Inbound owns no such thing and only needs to be
idempotent.

Manual approval is not a service — it is a human in a back-office UI reporting
through the same operation. Automated and human approvers are indistinguishable
to the orchestrator, which is the generality the model exists for.

## 10. Internal endpoints sit behind a shared secret

Internal operations live under `/internal/**`; the `SecurityFilterChain`
requires a configured secret header on that prefix while `/api/**` stays

This is where "no auth" stops being theoretical: an unauthenticated verdict
endpoint means anyone approves their own transfers and walks past fraud
detection entirely. It also gives the Spring Security chain one real rule to
enforce, which is what makes the whole configuration legible.

Not a contradiction of §2 — that declined to model *user* identity. This is
service-to-service trust across a boundary, a different concern created by the

## 11. Check services are pushed to, via the outbox

`CheckRequested` is a second event type on machinery the task's requirement 3
(*Rendszerintegráció*) demands regardless
("továbbítása … a külvilág felé" is a push). Marginal cost: one event type.

**Rejected — check services polling us.** It looks cheaper but is not: it costs
a query API, cursor semantics so a caller tracks what it has not seen, and
claim semantics so two Fraud Detection instances do not both grab the same
transfer — all *in addition to* the outbox. It also couples more tightly to a
service we do not control, requiring it to track cursors against our API.

## 12. Hand-rolled transactional outbox

An event row is written in the same transaction as the transfer, so neither can
exist without the other. A `@Scheduled` poller publishes unsent rows through a
one-method `EventPublisher` interface and marks them sent. At-least-once;
consumers must tolerate duplicates, which they must anyway.

**Kafka does not replace this.** "Commit to the database, then send to Kafka"
is still two writes with no transaction spanning them. Kafka is the transport
under `publish()`; the outbox is what makes the handoff atomic.

Hand-rolled (~55 lines) rather than adopting Spring Modulith's Event
Publication Registry, because the outbox is one of the few places the task asks
for demonstrated architectural judgement and a dependency demonstrates less of
it than code you can defend. Modulith and Kafka are named in the README as the
production answers — see [deferred.md](deferred.md).

In this build `publish()` writes a structured log line, and a profile-gated
`StubFraudDetection` consumes `CheckRequested` and reports a verdict a beat
later, so the async lifecycle is *visible* in the UI rather than taken on
faith. It can reject as well as approve, so the rejection path is demoable. It
is a fake consumer, not a fake mechanism — the outbox, ledger and verdict
endpoint it exercises are all real.

## 13. Balances: two fields on `Account`

`balance` (what the account holds) and `reservedAmount` (committed to in-flight
transfers). Available = `balance - reservedAmount`, which is the overdraft
check under the lock from §6. Reserving increments `reservedAmount`; settling
decrements both; rejecting or expiring decrements only `reservedAmount`.

This is the customer-facing model real banks present — "ledger balance" and
"available balance" are the industry terms, and a card authorization hold works
exactly this way.

What banks run *underneath* is double-entry: balances are a materialized
projection over a posting log, with internal accounts (suspense, clearing, FX
position) absorbing cross-currency differences so each currency's books balance
independently. Deferred deliberately — see [deferred.md](deferred.md).

## 14. Unanswered checks expire

Each check row carries a deadline. A `@Scheduled` reaper finds overdue
`PENDING` transfers, marks them `EXPIRED`, releases the reservation and
publishes the event.

Without it, a check that never responds leaves funds reserved forever with no
transaction to show for it — and `PENDING` would have no exit that does not
depend on an external service behaving. Cheap because the scheduled-poller
machinery already exists for the outbox.

A verdict arriving *after* expiry must not settle the transfer. Same
conditional-update guard as §5.

## 15. The FX rate is locked at request time

Fetched during creation, stored on the transfer with its fetch timestamp, used
at settlement.

The argument is failure handling, not accuracy. Fetching at settlement means
the flaky provider is called *after* every check has approved — a 503 there
leaves an approved transfer that cannot settle, with no caller to tell and no
one to retry, requiring a settlement retry queue and a policy for permanently
unsettleable transfers. Locking at request keeps the failure in front of the
caller, which is the "handle the flaky API elegantly" requirement, and keeps
the call in the position §4 put it.

Rate staleness on a long-pending transfer is already handled: **the quote's
validity window and the check deadline in §14 are the same clock.** A transfer
that outlives its quote expires and releases its funds. Whether to re-quote
instead is a business decision, not a technical one.

## 16. Money is a `long` count of minor units

`record Money(long minorUnits, Currency currency)`, as a JPA `@Embeddable` —
one record flattens to two columns. Amounts are counted in fillér and cents,
never in forints and euros.

**Rejected — `BigDecimal`.** The usual argument against it (float drift) does
not apply: `BigDecimal` is exact. The real problem is that it is
**unconstrained**. Nothing stops a mis-scaled column or a careless division
producing `100.505` HUF — a quantity that cannot exist. `long` fillér makes the
sub-unit *unrepresentable* rather than merely discouraged, and it leaves
exactly one place in the codebase where rounding happens.

It also removes a trap with no TypeScript equivalent: **`BigDecimal.equals`
compares scale**, so `new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00"))` is
`false` while `compareTo` says they are equal. Two amounts that are the same
money fail an equality assertion, and a `record`'s generated `equals` inherits
the problem.

- **Wire format is an integer count of minor units, in a field named
  `amountMinor`.** The name is the mitigation: `"amount": 10050` invites
  someone to read 10050 forints, `"amountMinor": 10050` does not.
- **Per-currency decimals (EUR/USD 2, HUF 0) live only at the edges** — form
  parsing and display. The core never divides by 100.
- **The rate stays `BigDecimal`.** It is the one value that is genuinely a
  decimal, and it is never money.
- `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN`, and **`422` when a converted amount rounds to
  zero** — 1 HUF to EUR would otherwise debit the source and credit nothing.

The single conversion, and the most error-prone line in the backend:

```
destMinor = round(srcMinor × rate × 10^(destScale − srcScale))
```

e.g. `10050 × 390.12 × 10^(0−2) = 39207.06 → 39207 Ft`. Table-test it: EUR→HUF,
HUF→EUR, USD→EUR, same-currency (no provider call at all), and round-to-zero.

**Honest consequence: money is not conserved across the two accounts.** The
rounding remainder vanishes. That is what the double-entry deferral costs — see
[deferred.md](deferred.md).

**Verify in the first hour:** Hibernate's support for `record` types as
`@Embeddable`. It has been supported since Hibernate 6.2 and Boot 4 ships
Hibernate 7, but a wrong assumption here re-shapes every entity.

## 17. One event stream, thin events, no catch-up

`GET /api/events/stream` — a single SSE endpoint, not one per transfer.
(SSE over WebSocket: the push described in the task's requirement 3 is
one-directional, and SSE reconnects on its own.)

**Liveness is scoped to the transfer submit flow only** — the `/transfers/:id`
screen. Accounts and Transactions refetch on navigation and on window focus.
Watching a balance tick live on a list nobody is looking at is not a
requirement.

Given that scope, a single endpoint wins for a small reason rather than a grand
one: one emitter registry plus a client-side `if (e.transferId !== mine) return`
is less machinery than a registry keyed by transfer ID with subscription
lifecycle and cleanup.

**No catch-up: no `Last-Event-ID`, no replay buffer, no outbox-as-event-log.**
The client refetches `GET /api/transfers/{id}` when the stream opens.

> The stream carries hints; the REST endpoint carries truth.

That converges from any missed state — a dropped connection, a server restart,
an event published before the browser subscribed — and it reuses the first-load
path rather than adding a second one. Transfer status is monotonic, so
subscribe-then-fetch needs no ordering logic: a stale fetch can only be
overtaken by a later invalidation.

**Event fatness is deliberately asymmetric**, and it looks like an
inconsistency unless it is stated:

| Direction | Shape | Why |
|---|---|---|
| SSE → browser | thin: `{ type, transferId }` | the browser can call our API |
| Outbox → services | fat: carries the payload | a consumer that must call back for the amount is exactly the coupling §11 rejected polling to avoid |

One named consequence of the narrow scope: after a terminal event the client
refetches accounts, so a balance the user just watched change is not stale when
they navigate away.

## 18. Errors are RFC 9457 `ProblemDetail`

`spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`; responses are
`application/problem+json`. **The `type` URN is the sole discriminator** — not
`type` *and* a `code` field, because two discriminators drift and eventually one
of them lies.

**Rejected — a hand-rolled error envelope.** Spring already emits
`ProblemDetail` for framework-level failures: `@Valid` rejections, `415`,
`405`, malformed JSON. Those responses are produced before any controller code
runs, so a custom envelope does not replace them — it ships a **second** error
shape alongside one you cannot switch off.

Attached to this:

- **`Retry-After` on the in-progress `409`, absent on the key-reuse `409`.**
  That gives [deferred.md](deferred.md)'s retry-semantics entry something
  concrete: the retryable case is machine-readably marked as such.
- **Field-level validation errors as an extension member.** Spring's default
  packs every violation into one unusable sentence; the form needs them per
  field.
- The client branches on `!response.ok` and parses one shape. Nothing else.

This supersedes §5's mention of a separate `code` field: the two `409` cases are
distinguished by their `type` URN (`urn:problem:request-in-progress` vs
`urn:problem:idempotency-key-reused`).

## 21. TanStack Router, and TanStack Query owns server state

**Router: TanStack Router**, chosen over React Router for typed route
configuration — a deliberate trade against familiarity and ecosystem size, not
a claim that it is the better library in general.

| Route | Screen |
|---|---|
| `/accounts` | list + create |
| `/transfers/new` | submit form |
| `/transfers/:id` | live status — the only SSE consumer |
| `/transfers` | the Transactions list |

Submitting navigates to `/transfers/:id`, so **pending state lives in the URL
rather than in transient component state** and survives a refresh. That is the
frontend half of §7.

Notes: TanStack Router needs `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json` or its
inference silently degrades; decide up front whether `routeTree.gen.ts` is
committed, because a half-committed generated file is a confusing diff.

**Query: TanStack Query.** The payoff of §17's thin events is that an SSE
message becomes nothing more than a **cache invalidation**:

```ts
queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['transfers', e.transferId] })
queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['accounts'] })
```

No merging, no reconciliation, no ordering logic. `refetchOnWindowFocus` (on by
default) quietly closes the scope hole §17 left on the other two screens.

Retry policy must be narrowed: `retry: (n, err) => n < 3 && err.status >= 500`.
Query's default retries anything — retrying a `422` is noise, and a `409
REQUEST_IN_PROGRESS` should wait for its `Retry-After` (§18), not Query's
backoff.
